sections.title: Sounds, letters and stress
sections.summary: Hungarian spelling is almost perfectly phonetic, so learning the letters, the short/long vowel pairs and the digraphs lets you read any word aloud. Stress is always on the first syllable.

rules.title: A Latin alphabet with extra letters
rules.body: Hungarian uses the Latin alphabet with 44 letters. The accented vowels (á, é, í, ó, ö, ő, ú, ü, ű) and the digraphs (cs, dz, dzs, gy, ly, ny, sz, ty, zs) count as letters in their own right with their own place in the alphabet, so 'sz' sorts after 's' and 'ö' after 'o'. Spelling is almost perfectly phonetic: each letter has one sound, and once you know the letters you can read any word aloud.

rules.title: Short and long vowels
rules.body: There are seven vowel pairs: a/á, e/é, i/í, o/ó, ö/ő, u/ú, ü/ű. The accent marks length, never stress. For i, o, ö, u and ü the long partner is simply held about twice as long. For a/á and e/é the quality changes too: 'a' is a short rounded vowel like the 'o' in British 'hot', 'á' is the open 'a' of 'father'; 'e' is like 'e' in 'bed', 'é' is a long closed 'ay' without the glide. Length distinguishes words.

examples.en: he is glad – he goes mad

rules.title: The digraphs
rules.body: Two or three letters can spell one sound. cs is 'ch' as in church (csak), sz is 's' as in sun (szép), zs is the 's' of measure (zseb), gy is a soft 'dy' with the tongue on the palate (gyerek), ny is the 'ny' of canyon (nyár), ty is a soft 'ty' (tyúk), ly is pronounced exactly like j, that is English 'y' (lyuk, hely), and dzs is 'j' as in jam (dzsem).

rules.title: The s / sz trap
rules.body: A single 's' is always 'sh' (sok, sör, Budapest sounds like 'buda-pesht'), while 'sz' is the plain 's' of English (szia, szeretlek). English speakers constantly swap these two. Similarly 'c' is 'ts' as in cats (cica, utca), 'j' is 'y' as in yes (jó), and 'z' is a normal 'z'. The letter 'y' on its own appears only in digraphs and old family names.

rules.title: Stress is always on the first syllable
rules.body: Every Hungarian word is stressed on its first syllable, no matter how many suffixes are added. Compounds carry a lighter secondary stress on the second element. Unstressed vowels keep their full quality; there is no reduction to a schwa as in English, so 'tanulok' has three clear vowels. The pitch of a yes/no question rises on the second-to-last syllable and falls on the last.

rules.title: Long consonants
rules.body: A doubled consonant is held noticeably longer, and length can change the meaning. A digraph is doubled by doubling only its first letter: ssz, ccs, ggy, nny, tty.

rules.title: The rounded front vowels ö, ő, ü, ű
rules.body: These sounds do not exist in standard English. 'ü' is 'ee' said with rounded lips, like German ü or French 'u'; 'ö' is like German ö or the vowel of French 'peu'. 'ő' and 'ű' are the same sounds held long. They are very common, so practise them early.

rules.title: A few other consonants
rules.body: 'r' is rolled or tapped as in Spanish. 'h' is always pronounced at the start of a syllable, but is silent at the end of a handful of words (cseh, méh). 'v' is an ordinary v. The letters w, x and q appear only in foreign words and names, and 'ch' in loanwords is pronounced like h (technika).

exercises.q: Which syllable of a Hungarian word is stressed?
options: it varies from word to word
exercises.explain: Hungarian stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word.

exercises.q: Which letter is pronounced like English 'sh'?
exercises.explain: A single s is 'sh'; sz is the plain English s.

exercises.q: Hungarian 'sz' sounds like the 's' in English 'sun'.
exercises.explain: sz is the plain s sound; it is single s that sounds like 'sh'.

options: a soft 'dy' with the tongue on the palate
exercises.explain: gy is a palatal stop, roughly 'dy' said in one movement, as in 'gyerek' or 'magyar'.

exercises.q: Write the long partner of the vowel 'o': ___
exercises.explain: The acute accent marks a long vowel: o/ó.

exercises.q: The accent on 'á' shows that the syllable is stressed.
exercises.explain: Accents mark vowel length (and for a/á, e/é a different quality); stress is always on the first syllable anyway.

exercises.q: Which word contains a long vowel?
exercises.explain: Only kór has an accented, long vowel; kor/kór differ in meaning only by length.

exercises.q: Write the digraph that spells the 'ch' sound of 'church': ___
exercises.explain: cs = ch, as in 'csak' (only) and 'család' (family).

exercises.q: How is 'ly' pronounced in standard Hungarian today, as in 'lyuk' (hole)?
exercises.explain: In the standard language ly and j are pronounced identically, as English y.
c is always 'ts': cica, utca, Vác.

exercises.q: What is the difference in sound between 'hal' (fish) and 'hall' (he hears)?
options: the l is held longer in hall
the a is long in hall
the stress moves to the end
exercises.explain: Doubled consonants are pronounced long, and this alone can distinguish words.

exercises.q: Write the doubled form of 'sz' as it appears in 'hosszú' (long): ___
exercises.explain: A digraph is doubled by doubling only its first letter: sz becomes ssz.

exercises.q: Which pair of words differs only by vowel length?
exercises.explain: e/é is a short/long pair; the other pairs change the vowel itself.

exercises.q: Like English, Hungarian reduces unstressed vowels to a weak 'uh' sound.
exercises.explain: Every vowel keeps its full quality whether stressed or not.

exercises.q: The short vowel 'a' has a long partner that sounds like the 'a' of 'father'. Write it: ___
exercises.explain: a and á differ both in length and in quality.

exercises.q: 'szeretlek' (I love you) has how many syllables, and which one is stressed?
exercises.explain: sze-ret-lek has three syllables and, like every word, is stressed on the first.

exercises.en: Good morning! (literally: I wish a good morning)

exercises.explain: ny is a palatal n, as in nyár (summer) or lány (girl).

exercises.q: Which word begins with the sound of English 'ch'?
exercises.explain: cs = ch; sz = s, zs = zh, s = sh.

exercises.q: Write the long form of the vowel 'ü': ___
exercises.explain: The double acute marks the long rounded front vowels: ö/ő and ü/ű.

pairs: begins with the ny of canyon
begins with the zh of measure

exercises.q: Which group contains the rounded front vowels, similar to German ö and ü?
exercises.explain: ö, ő, ü and ű are pronounced with rounded lips and the tongue forward.

exercises.q: In 'Magyarország' the main stress falls on the third syllable, 'or'.
exercises.explain: The main stress is on 'Ma', the first syllable; 'ország' only carries a lighter secondary stress.

exercises.q: Complete the spelling of 'beautiful' with the right digraph: ___ép
exercises.explain: szép begins with the plain s sound, spelled sz.

exercises.q: The trigraph 'dzs', as in 'dzsem' (jam), sounds like:
exercises.explain: dzs is the voiced counterpart of cs, i.e. English j.

sections.title: Vowel harmony
sections.summary: Almost every suffix comes in two or three forms, and the vowels of the word decide which one is attached. Mastering this early makes every later chapter easier.

rules.title: Two classes of vowels
rules.body: Vowels are either back (a, á, o, ó, u, ú) or front (e, é, i, í, ö, ő, ü, ű). Most words contain only back vowels or only front vowels, and are called back words or front words. Front vowels are further split into unrounded (e, é, i, í) and rounded (ö, ő, ü, ű).

rules.title: Suffixes echo the word
rules.body: Suffixes come in sets whose vowels match the word they attach to: a back word takes the back form, a front word the front form. The two-form set -ban/-ben (in) is the classic example. You never mix classes inside one word, so 'házben' is impossible.

rules.title: Two-form suffixes
rules.body: Most suffixes have a back form with a or o and a front form with e or ö: -ban/-ben (in), -ba/-be (into), -ból/-ből (out of), -nak/-nek (to, for), -ra/-re (onto), -ról/-ről (off, about), -tól/-től (from), -nál/-nél (at), -val/-vel (with). A few suffixes have only one form and never change: -ig (until), -ért (for), -kor (at a time), -ként (as).

examples.en: out of the town, out of the garden
as far as the house, as far as the garden (one form)

rules.title: Three-form suffixes
rules.body: Some suffixes distinguish three vowels: o for back words, e for front unrounded words, ö for front rounded words. Look at the last vowel of the word to choose between e and ö. Examples are -hoz/-hez/-höz (to), -on/-en/-ön (on), -ok/-ek/-ök (plural and 'I' on verbs), -tok/-tek/-tök and -szor/-szer/-ször (times).

examples.en: on the table, on the chair, on the ground

examples.target: a házhoz, a kerthez, a tükörhöz
examples.en: to the house, to the garden, to the mirror

rules.title: Mixed words
rules.body: Words containing both back and front vowels usually follow the last vowel. If the last vowel is i, í or é after a back vowel, the word is treated as back: kocsiban, papíron, kávéban. If the last vowel is ö, ő, ü or ű the word is front: sofőrnek. Words whose last vowel is e are mostly front, especially foreign words and compounds: hotelben, Budapesten. Exceptions exist, so note the -ban/-ben form when you learn a mixed word.

rules.title: Words with only i, í or é
rules.body: Words whose only vowels are i, í or é are front words in the great majority of cases: vízben (in water), kézben (in the hand), szívnek (to the heart). A small historical group takes back suffixes and simply has to be learnt: híd (bridge), sír (grave), nyíl (arrow), cél (aim), zsír (fat), and verbs like ír (write), nyit (open), iszik (drink), sír (cry).

rules.title: Compound words follow their last part
rules.body: In a compound only the final element matters, because the suffix attaches to it. Budapest is Buda + Pest, so it takes front suffixes; könyvtár (library) ends in tár and takes back suffixes.

rules.title: Harmony runs through the whole word
rules.body: When several suffixes are stacked, every one of them harmonizes with the stem. Verb endings harmonize too: 'I' is -ok, -ek or -ök and 'we' is -unk or -ünk. The system is automatic once you know the stem's class, so always learn whether a word is back or front.

examples.en: in my house, in my garden
I study, I ask for, I sit

exercises.q: Which group lists the back vowels?
options: a á o ó u ú
exercises.explain: Back vowels are a, á, o, ó, u, ú; all the others are front.
ház is a back word, so it takes the back form -ban.
kert has a front vowel, so the suffix is -ben.

exercises.q: 'könyvban' is the correct form of 'in a book'.
exercises.explain: könyv is a front word; the correct form is könyvben.
Péter has only front vowels, so it takes -nek.
autó is a back word (a, ó), so it takes -nak.

exercises.en: The book is in the bag.

exercises.explain: The last vowel ö is front rounded, so the three-form suffix takes -höz.
é is front unrounded, so the linking vowel is e: széken.

exercises.q: In mixed words like 'kávé' the suffix is usually back: kávéban.
exercises.explain: A final é after a back vowel does not change the word's back class.
A final ő makes a mixed word front, so it takes -nek.

exercises.q: Which of these i-vowel words takes BACK suffixes?
exercises.explain: híd belongs to the small historical group of back words: hídon, hídnak.
híd is one of the exceptional i-words that take back suffixes.

exercises.q: A compound word harmonizes according to its last element, so könyvtár (library) gives könyvtárban.
exercises.explain: Only the final element, tár, decides the suffix form.
The last element út is back, so the suffix is -on.
tanul is a back word, so the ending is -ok.
ü is front rounded, so the three-form ending is -ök.
The 'we' ending has two forms, -unk/-ünk; kér is front so it takes -ünk.

exercises.q: A word may mix back and front suffix forms, for example 'házben'.
exercises.explain: Every suffix must agree with the stem; ház takes only back forms like házban.
Foreign words ending in a syllable with e are normally treated as front: hotelben.

exercises.q: Budapest takes front suffixes: Budapesten, Budapestre.
exercises.explain: The last element Pest has a front vowel, so the compound is front.
tanár contains only back vowels, so it takes -nak.
The last vowel ö is front rounded, so the linking vowel is ö.

exercises.answer: A tanár egy könyvet ad a gyereknek.
exercises.en: The teacher gives the child a book.

exercises.q: Words containing only e, é, i or í take front suffixes in the great majority of cases, e.g. kézben, vízben.
exercises.explain: Only a short list of i/í/é words (híd, sír, nyíl, cél...) is back.

sections.title: Articles, nouns and plurals
sections.summary: Hungarian has no grammatical gender, a definite article with two shapes (a/az), an indefinite article that doubles as 'one', and a plural in -k that needs a linking vowel after consonants.

rules.title: The definite article: a / az
rules.body: 'The' is a before a consonant and az before a vowel, exactly like English a/an but for the definite article. Hungarian uses the definite article more than English: with abstract nouns, with possessed nouns (a könyvem, my book) and, in everyday speech, often before people's names.

rules.title: The indefinite article: egy
rules.body: egy means both 'a/an' and 'one'. It is used less than in English: it is dropped before professions, nationalities and other categories after 'to be', and before nouns in a general sense. Keep it when you mean 'a certain one' or 'one of'.

rules.title: No grammatical gender
rules.body: Nouns have no gender, adjectives never agree in gender, and a single pronoun ő means both 'he' and 'she'. Natural sex is shown only by vocabulary (férfi man, nő woman) or by compounds with -nő (tanárnő, female teacher).

examples.en: He is a doctor. / She is a doctor.

rules.title: The plural ending -k after a vowel
rules.body: The plural is -k. After a vowel it attaches directly. A final short a or e lengthens to á or é before any suffix, including -k.

rules.title: Linking vowels after a consonant
rules.body: After a consonant a linking vowel is needed: -ok for back words, -ek for front unrounded, -ök for front rounded. Beware of two irregularities: a sizeable group of back words takes -ak instead of -ok (ház – házak, fal – falak, hal – halak, láb – lábak), and some ö/ü words take -ek rather than -ök (könyv – könyvek, föld – földek). The same linking vowel reappears in the accusative, so learn it with the noun.

rules.title: Stems that change before the plural
rules.body: Some nouns alter their shape before -k. A long á or é in the last syllable may shorten: kéz – kezek, víz – vizek, madár – madarak, kenyér – kenyerek, út – utak, tűz – tüzek. Some drop a vowel: bokor – bokrok, tükör – tükrök. Nouns ending in a long vowel sometimes add v and shorten: ló – lovak, kő – kövek, tó – tavak, fű – füvek. These stem changes show up before most other suffixes too.

rules.title: No plural after numbers and quantity words
rules.body: After a number or a quantity word (sok many, kevés few, néhány a few, hány? how many?, minden every) the noun stays singular. 'Two' is két before a noun and kettő standing alone.

rules.title: Paired body parts are singular
rules.body: Eyes, ears, hands and feet are treated as a single unit: szem (eye), fül (ear), kéz (hand), láb (foot/leg) are used in the singular when you mean both. 'One eye' is fél szem, literally 'half an eye'.

examples.en: My legs hurt. / My leg hurts.

rules.title: This and that: ez / az with the article
rules.body: The demonstratives ez (this) and az (that) are followed by the definite article when they stand before a noun: ez a ház, az az autó. Their plurals are ezek and azok, and the noun is then plural too. Used alone as a pronoun they take no article: Ez könyv. (This is a book.)

exercises.explain: az is used before a vowel.
ház begins with a consonant, so the article is a.
óra begins with a vowel, so the article is az.

exercises.q: Hungarian nouns have grammatical gender, as in German or French.
exercises.explain: Hungarian has no gender; even 'he' and 'she' are the same word, ő.
A final a lengthens to á before the plural -k.
After a vowel the plural -k attaches directly.
ház belongs to the group of back words that take the linking vowel a.
könyv takes -ek despite its ö; this must be learnt with the word.

exercises.q: After a number the noun stays singular: három könyv.
exercises.explain: Numbers and quantity words are followed by the singular.
No plural after a number: három alma.
sok (many) is a quantity word, so the noun remains singular.
The long í shortens before the plural: vizek.
The numeral one and the indefinite article are the same word.

exercises.q: The usual way to state your profession, 'I am a teacher':
exercises.explain: No article is used before a profession after 'to be'.
The last vowel ö is front rounded, so the linking vowel is ö.
A demonstrative before a noun is followed by the article: ez a ház.
ez/ezek and az/azok; the noun after them is plural too: ezek a házak.
The demonstrative agrees in number: ezek a könyvek.
hal is one of the back nouns with linking vowel a: halak, halat.

exercises.q: Hány ___ van? (How many books are there? könyv)
exercises.explain: hány? (how many?) is followed by a singular noun.

exercises.q: 'az' is used before a word starting with a vowel and 'a' before a consonant.
exercises.explain: The choice depends only on the following sound, like English a/an.
bokor drops its second o before the plural: bokrok.
tó is a v-stem: it shortens and adds v before the plural, like ló – lovak.

exercises.q: 'Fáj a szemem' (my eyes hurt) uses the singular szem even for both eyes.
exercises.explain: Paired body parts are normally singular in Hungarian.

sections.title: 'To be', pronouns and possession
sections.summary: The verb 'to be' is often dropped in the third person, possession is marked by endings on the possessed noun, and 'I have' is expressed as 'to me there is'.

rules.title: Personal pronouns
rules.body: The pronouns are én (I), te (you, singular informal), ő (he/she), mi (we), ti (you, plural informal), ők (they). Because the verb ending shows the person, subject pronouns are normally left out and used only for emphasis or contrast. The formal 'you' is Ön (plural Önök) or the slightly less formal maga/maguk; both take third-person verb forms.

examples.en: I am Hungarian, he is English.

rules.title: The present tense of lenni (to be)
rules.body: vagyok (I am), vagy (you are), van (he/she/it is), vagyunk (we are), vagytok (you are), vannak (they are). The infinitive is lenni. The negative of van and vannak is nincs and nincsenek; the other persons just take nem: nem vagyok.

rules.title: When van and vannak are dropped
rules.body: In the third person, van/vannak is omitted when the predicate is a noun or an adjective: Ő tanár. A ház nagy. It is kept when it means 'is located' or 'exists', and when a place or time is stated: A könyv az asztalon van. The first and second persons always keep the verb: Tanár vagyok.

examples.en: There is a shop on the corner.

rules.title: nincs and nincsenek
rules.body: 'Is not (there)' and 'are not (there)' are nincs and nincsenek, which replace nem van and nem vannak. They are used for location and existence and for the negative of 'to have'. With a noun or adjective predicate you simply use nem: Ő nem tanár.

rules.title: Predicate nouns and adjectives agree in number
rules.body: When the subject is plural, a predicate noun or adjective takes the plural -k as well: Ők diákok. A házak nagyok. With the first and second persons plural the verb is also present: Mi diákok vagyunk.

rules.title: Possessive endings: my, your, his/her
rules.body: Possession is shown by an ending on the possessed noun, not by a separate word. Singular possessors: -m (my), -d (your), -a/-e or -ja/-je (his/her). After a consonant, -m and -d need a linking vowel (-om/-em/-öm, -od/-ed/-öd, or -am/-ad in the a-group of nouns). A final a or e lengthens. Whether the third person takes -a/-e or -ja/-je has to be learnt: vowel-final nouns always take -ja/-je.

examples.en: my house, your house, his/her house
my book, your book, his/her book
my car, your car, his/her car
my dog, your dog, his/her dog

rules.title: Possessive endings: our, your, their
rules.body: Plural possessors: -unk/-ünk (our), -tok/-tek/-tök with a linking vowel after a consonant (your), -uk/-ük or -juk/-jük (their). Nouns that take -ja in the third person singular take -juk/-jük in the plural.

examples.en: our house, your house, their house
our book, your book, their book
our car, your car, their car

rules.title: Possessor nouns and possessive pronouns
rules.body: 'Péter's book' puts the possessor first, unmarked, and the possessive ending on the thing possessed: Péter könyve. The dative -nak/-nek can be added to the possessor for emphasis or when the possessor is separated: Péternek a könyve. Standalone possessive pronouns ('mine', 'yours') are az enyém, a tiéd, az övé, a miénk, a tiétek, az övék.

rules.title: 'I have': nekem van
rules.body: There is no verb 'to have'. You say 'to me there is a ...-of-mine': (Nekem) van egy kutyám. The dative pronoun (nekem, neked, neki, nekünk, nektek, nekik) is optional and adds emphasis; the possessive ending on the noun is obligatory. The negative uses nincs/nincsenek. With a named possessor use the dative: Péternek van autója.

rules.title: Plural possessed things
rules.body: When several things are possessed, an -i- is inserted before the person ending: házaim (my houses), könyveid (your books), barátai (his/her friends), autóink (our cars). The plural -k is not used here.

exercises.explain: vagyok is the first person singular of lenni.
The second person singular of 'to be' is vagy.

exercises.q: 'Ő tanár van.' is the correct way to say 'He is a teacher'.
exercises.explain: With a noun predicate the third-person van is dropped: Ő tanár.
van is kept when it expresses location.
ház belongs to the a-group, so the linking vowel is a: házam, házak, házat.
könyv takes the linking vowel e: könyvem.
Vowel-final nouns take -ja/-je in the third person.
kert is a front word, so the linking vowel is e: kerted.

exercises.q: 'Nekem van' literally means 'to me there is' and is how Hungarian says 'I have'.
exercises.explain: Hungarian has no verb 'to have'; possession uses the dative plus van.
The negative of van is nincs, never nem van.
The 'our' ending is -unk/-ünk; ház is back, so házunk.
autó takes -ja in the singular and therefore -juk in the plural; it is a back word.

exercises.q: 'Ők diák.' is correct for 'They are students'.
exercises.explain: A predicate noun agrees in number: Ők diákok.
The possessor is unmarked and the possessed noun takes -e: Péter könyve.
kutya lengthens its final a and takes -ja: kutyája.
az enyém = mine, a tiéd = yours, az övé = his/hers.

exercises.q: Van/vannak is dropped in the third person before a noun or adjective, but kept when stating where something is.
exercises.explain: Ő tanár, but Ő otthon van.

exercises.q: A könyvek az asztalon ___. (The books are on the table.)
exercises.explain: Location requires the verb, and a plural subject takes vannak.
After a consonant the -tok/-tek/-tök ending needs a linking vowel: könyvetek.
Plural possessed things take -i- before the person ending: barátaim.

exercises.q: 'Ön' is a formal 'you' and takes third-person verb forms, as in 'Ön tanár?'.
exercises.explain: Ön and Önök are grammatically third person.
The adjective takes the plural with a plural subject, and 'we' needs vagyunk.
idő + -d gives időd; 'van időd?' is 'do you have time?'.

sections.title: The present tense: indefinite and definite conjugation
sections.summary: Hungarian verbs have two sets of present-tense endings: the indefinite set, used with no object or an indefinite one, and the definite set, used when the object is definite. Choosing between them is the heart of Hungarian verb grammar.

rules.title: Dictionary form and infinitive
rules.body: The dictionary form of a verb is the third person singular present, which has no ending: tanul (studies), kér (asks for), ül (sits). The infinitive adds -ni: tanulni, kérni, ülni; stems ending in two consonants or in -ít insert a linking vowel: mondani, érteni, tanítani. Verbs listed with -ik, like lakik (lives) or eszik (eats), form a special group.

rules.title: The indefinite endings
rules.body: Indefinite present endings: -ok/-ek/-ök (I), -sz (you), no ending (he/she), -unk/-ünk (we), -tok/-tek/-tök (you plural), -nak/-nek (they). They harmonize with the stem.

examples.target: tanulok, tanulsz, tanul, tanulunk, tanultok, tanulnak
examples.en: I study, you study, he studies, we study, you study, they study

examples.target: kérek, kérsz, kér, kérünk, kértek, kérnek
examples.en: I ask for, you ask for, ...

examples.target: ülök, ülsz, ül, ülünk, ültök, ülnek

rules.title: Adjustments in the 'you' form
rules.body: After stems ending in s, sz or z the second person singular ending is -ol/-el/-öl instead of -sz: olvasol (you read), nézel (you watch), főzöl (you cook), hozol (you bring). After stems ending in two consonants or in -ít, -sz takes a linking vowel: mondasz, értesz, tanítasz. The same stems take a linking vowel before -tok and -nak: mondotok, mondanak.

rules.title: -ik verbs
rules.body: Verbs whose dictionary form ends in -ik (lakik, eszik, iszik, dolgozik, alszik) keep -ik in the third person singular, and in careful standard speech take -om/-em/-öm in the first person singular: lakom, eszem, iszom, dolgozom. In everyday speech lakok, eszek are common but still regarded as substandard. The second person takes -ol/-el/-öl: laksz is fine but eszel, iszol, dolgozol.

rules.title: When the object is definite
rules.body: The definite conjugation is used when the verb has a definite direct object: a noun with a/az, a proper name, a noun with a possessive ending, ezt/azt (this/that), the third-person pronouns őt, őket, Önt, and clauses introduced by hogy. The indefinite conjugation is used with no object, with egy + noun, bare or numbered nouns, with mit?, valamit, and with the first and second person objects engem, téged, minket, titeket.

examples.en: What would you like? – I'd like coffee.

rules.title: The definite endings
rules.body: Definite present endings: -om/-em/-öm (I), -od/-ed/-öd (you), -ja/-i (he/she), -juk/-jük (we), -játok/-itek (you plural), -ják/-ik (they). Back verbs use the j-forms, front verbs the i-forms.

examples.target: tanulom, tanulod, tanulja, tanuljuk, tanuljátok, tanulják
examples.en: I study it, you study it, ...

examples.target: kérem, kéred, kéri, kérjük, kéritek, kérik
examples.en: I ask for it, you ask for it, ...

rules.title: The j of the definite endings assimilates
rules.body: After stems ending in s, sz, z or dz the j of -ja, -juk, -játok, -ják becomes a doubling of that consonant: olvassa (he reads it), olvassuk, nézzük (we watch it), hozza (he brings it), mossuk (we wash it).

rules.title: The -lak/-lek ending: 'I ... you'
rules.body: When the subject is 'I' and the object is 'you' (singular or plural informal), the verb takes the special ending -lak/-lek: szeretlek (I love you), látlak (I see you), kérlek (I ask you, please), várlak (I'm waiting for you). After a stem ending in two consonants a linking vowel appears: értelek (I understand you), while hívlak and nézlek need none.

rules.title: Common irregular verbs
rules.body: A handful of everyday verbs have irregular stems. megy (go): megyek, mész, megy, megyünk, mentek, mennek. jön (come): jövök, jössz, jön, jövünk, jöttök, jönnek. eszik (eat): eszem, eszel, eszik, eszünk, esztek, esznek. iszik (drink): iszom, iszol, iszik, iszunk, isztok, isznak. tesz, vesz, visz (put, take/buy, carry): teszek, teszel, tesz, teszünk, tesztek, tesznek. alszik (sleep): alszom, alszol, alszik, alszunk, alszotok, alszanak. The present tense also serves for the future with a time word: Holnap megyek.

examples.en: Tomorrow we are going to the cinema.

exercises.explain: With no object the indefinite form tanulok is used; tanulom would mean 'I study it'.
The indefinite second person ending is -sz: kérsz.
After s, sz or z the 'you' ending is -ol/-el/-öl, not -sz.
The 'we' ending is -unk/-ünk; ül is front, so ülünk.

exercises.q: Which object requires the DEFINITE conjugation?
exercises.explain: A noun with the definite article a/az is a definite object.
'a házat' is definite, so the verb must be látom.

exercises.q: ___ a könyvet. (I am reading the book; olvas)
exercises.explain: Definite object, first person: olvasom.
-lak/-lek marks an 'I' subject with a 'you' object.
-ik verbs take -om/-em/-öm in the first person singular.
The stem is esz-; 'we' is eszünk.
The definite -juk/-jük assimilates after z: nézzük.
megy is irregular: megyek, mész, megy, megyünk, mentek, mennek.

exercises.q: 'mész' is the second person singular of 'megy' (go).
exercises.explain: Hová mész? = Where are you going?
The third person plural is jönnek; the v-stem appears only in jövök and jövünk.

exercises.q: ___ téged. (I am waiting for you; vár)
exercises.explain: 'I ... you' takes the ending -lak/-lek: várlak.
The stem esz- is front: esznek. eszik is the third person singular.

exercises.q: An object with 'egy' (a/an) takes the definite conjugation.
exercises.explain: egy + noun is indefinite: Olvasok egy könyvet.

exercises.q: Ő ___ a könyvet. (He is reading the book; olvas)
exercises.explain: The definite -ja assimilates after s: olvassa.
A stem ending in two consonants needs a linking vowel before -sz: mondasz.
alszik is an -ik verb, so the standard first person is alszom.

exercises.q: The present tense can refer to the future when a time word is present: 'Holnap megyek.'
exercises.explain: Hungarian often uses the present for planned future actions.

exercises.en: Tomorrow we are going to the cinema.

exercises.q: Which pronoun object takes the INDEFINITE conjugation?
exercises.explain: First and second person objects (engem, téged, minket, titeket) count as indefinite.
-juk assimilates to the final z: hozzuk.
After sz the 'you' ending is -el; teszed is the definite form.

sections.title: The main cases, part 1
sections.summary: Hungarian marks the role of a noun with suffixes instead of prepositions. This chapter covers the accusative, the dative and the nine place suffixes that form three neat trios: inside, on the surface and near.

rules.title: The accusative -t
rules.body: The direct object takes -t. After a vowel it attaches directly, and a final a or e lengthens: autót, kutyát, kefét. After most consonants it needs a linking vowel, -ot/-et/-öt, or -at in the a-group nouns that also take -ak in the plural: házat, falat, halat. After l, r, n, ny, s, sz, z, zs and j the -t usually attaches directly: asztalt, tanárt, bort, sört, pénzt. Stem changes seen in the plural reappear: kezet, vizet, kenyeret, lovat.

rules.title: Accusative of pronouns and plurals
rules.body: The pronoun objects are engem (me), téged (you), őt (him/her), minket (us), titeket (you), őket (them), Önt/Önöket (you, formal). Demonstratives become ezt and azt, the question words kit? and mit?. Plural nouns add -at/-et after the plural -k: könyveket, házakat, autókat.

rules.title: The dative -nak/-nek
rules.body: The dative marks the indirect object, the person something is given, said or shown to. It is also the case of the possessor in 'to have' sentences and is required by kell (need), tetszik (please, like) and many others. The dative pronouns are nekem, neked, neki, nekünk, nektek, nekik.

rules.title: Inside: -ban/-ben, -ba/-be, -ból/-ből
rules.body: Place suffixes come in trios of location, movement towards and movement away. For the inside of something: -ban/-ben (in), -ba/-be (into), -ból/-ből (out of). Learners often mix up -ban and -ba; remember that the longer form is the static one.

examples.en: I come out of the room.

rules.title: On the surface: -n/-on/-en/-ön, -ra/-re, -ról/-ről
rules.body: For a surface: -n (after a vowel) or -on/-en/-ön (on), -ra/-re (onto), -ról/-ről (off, down from). -ról/-ről also means 'about': a filmről beszélünk. A final a or e lengthens before these suffixes: kutyán, szobára, Budán.

examples.en: The book is on the table.
I put the book onto the table.
I take the book off the table.

rules.title: Near: -nál/-nél, -hoz/-hez/-höz, -tól/-től
rules.body: For the vicinity of something, and for people: -nál/-nél (at, by, at someone's place), -hoz/-hez/-höz (to, up to), -tól/-től (from, away from). These are the suffixes for going to see people and institutions: az orvoshoz, Péternél, a tanártól.

examples.en: I am going to the doctor.
I got a letter from Anna.
I am sitting by the window.

rules.title: Town and country names
rules.body: Most Hungarian towns take the surface trio: Budapesten, Szegedre, Pécsről. Towns ending in -n, -ny, -m, -i, -r and a few others take the inside trio instead: Debrecenben, Győrbe, Sopronból, Veszprémben. Foreign cities and all countries take the inside trio: Londonban, Bécsben, Angliában, Németországba. The one big exception is Magyarország itself: Magyarországon, Magyarországra.

rules.title: Case suffixes on pronouns
rules.body: Case suffixes cannot attach to én, te, ő; instead the suffix becomes a stem and takes possessive-style endings. 'In me' is bennem, benned, benne, bennünk, bennetek, bennük; 'at me' is nálam, nálad, nála, nálunk, nálatok, náluk; and likewise hozzám (to me), tőlem (from me), rám (onto me), rólam (about me), belőlem (out of me), belém (into me).

examples.en: He is sleeping at our place.

rules.title: Verbs that choose a case
rules.body: Many verbs require a particular case where English uses a preposition or nothing at all. gondol -ra/-re (think of), vár -ra/-re (wait for), emlékszik -ra/-re (remember), beszél -ról/-ről (talk about), fél -tól/-től (be afraid of), kérdez -tól/-től (ask someone), segít -nak/-nek (help someone), örül -nak/-nek (be glad of). Learn the case together with the verb.

examples.en: I am waiting for the bus.
I am afraid of the dog.

exercises.explain: After a vowel the -t attaches directly.

exercises.q: Kérek egy ___. (I'd like a beer; sör)
exercises.explain: After r the accusative -t attaches directly: sört.
ház is an a-group noun: házak, házat.

exercises.q: The direct object ending is -t, sometimes preceded by a linking vowel.
exercises.explain: autót, asztalt, könyvet, házat all carry the accusative -t.

exercises.q: Látlak ___. (I see you; accusative of te)
exercises.explain: The object form of te is téged.
engem is the accusative; nekem is 'to me', velem is 'with me'.
-ban/-ben is the static 'in'; -ba/-be is 'into'.

exercises.q: Bemegyek a ___. (I go into the shop; bolt)
exercises.explain: Movement into something takes -ba/-be: boltba.
-ból/-ből expresses movement out of.
-ban/-ben is static 'in'; movement into is -ba/-be.
-on/-en/-ön is static 'on'.

exercises.q: Felteszem a könyvet a ___. (I put the book onto the shelf; polc)
exercises.explain: Movement onto a surface takes -ra/-re.

exercises.q: Beszélünk a ___. (We are talking about the film; film)
exercises.explain: -ról/-ről means 'about' as well as 'off'.

exercises.en: The cat is on the table.

exercises.explain: -nál/-nél means 'at, by, at someone's place'.

exercises.q: Megyek az ___. (I am going to the doctor; orvos)
exercises.explain: Going to a person takes -hoz/-hez/-höz.
-tól/-től is 'from' a person or place.
Budapest takes the surface suffix: Budapesten.
Towns ending in -n take the inside trio: Debrecenben.
Foreign cities take -ban/-ben.
Magyarország is the exception among countries and takes -on.

exercises.en: Tomorrow I am travelling to Szeged.

exercises.explain: nálam is -nál with the first person ending; bennem = in me, hozzám = to me.

exercises.q: Rád ___. (I am thinking of you; gondol)
exercises.explain: gondol takes -ra/-re; rád is 'onto you'.

exercises.q: 'Félek a kutyától' means 'I am afraid of the dog' and uses -tól/-től.
exercises.explain: fél (be afraid) governs -tól/-től.

exercises.q: Várok a ___. (I am waiting for the bus; busz)
exercises.explain: vár (wait for) governs -ra/-re.

exercises.q: Megyek ___. (I am going to Péter's; Péter)
exercises.explain: Going to a person takes -hoz/-hez/-höz; Péter is front, so -hez.

sections.title: Cases, part 2 and postpositions
sections.summary: The remaining common case suffixes (with, for, until, as, at a time) and the postpositions that follow a noun instead of preceding it. Many postpositions come in three-way sets and take personal endings.

rules.title: -val/-vel: with
rules.body: 'With' is -val/-vel. After a vowel it attaches directly and a final a or e lengthens: autóval, Annával. After a consonant the v assimilates to that consonant, which is written double: Péterrel, késsel, busszal, villamossal, kézzel, a barátommal. The pronoun forms are velem, veled, vele, velünk, veletek, velük.

rules.title: -ért: for
rules.body: -ért means 'for' in the sense of purpose or exchange: going for bread, paying for a ticket. It has one form only. On pronouns: értem, érted, érte, értünk, értetek, értük. Miért? (why?) and ezért/azért (that is why) are built on it.

examples.en: I am going out for bread.
How much did you pay for the ticket?

rules.title: -ig: until, as far as
rules.body: -ig expresses the end point in space or time: Budapestig (as far as Budapest), ötig (until five), estig (until evening). It has one form. Related words: meddig? (how far, how long?), eddig (until now), addig (until then).

examples.en: I travel as far as Szeged.

rules.title: -ként and -ul/-ül: as, in a language
rules.body: -ként means 'as, in the role of': tanárként (as a teacher), turistaként (as a tourist). -ul/-ül is the suffix of languages and manner: magyarul (in Hungarian), angolul, németül; and manner words such as rosszul (badly); jól (well) is irregular.

rules.title: -kor: at a time
rules.body: -kor gives the time at which something happens and has a single form: ötkor (at five), hat órakor (at six o'clock), fél hatkor (at half past five), karácsonykor (at Christmas). mikor? is 'when?' and akkor is 'then, at that time'.

examples.en: When are you coming? – At eight.
At Christmas we are at home.

rules.title: Postpositions follow the noun
rules.body: Where English has prepositions, Hungarian has postpositions placed after the noun. The noun itself stays in its basic form. Common ones: mellett (beside), előtt (in front of, before), mögött (behind), alatt (under), fölött or felett (above), között (between), után (after), körül (around), nélkül (without), miatt (because of), helyett (instead of), szerint (according to), felé (towards), ellen (against).

rules.title: Three-way postpositions
rules.body: Like the place suffixes, the spatial postpositions have a static form in -tt, a 'towards' form in -é and a 'from' form in -ól/-ől/-ül: mellett / mellé / mellől, előtt / elé / elől, mögött / mögé / mögül, alatt / alá / alól, fölött / fölé / fölül, között / közé / közül. Use the -é form with verbs of putting and going.

examples.target: A szék az asztal mellett van.
examples.en: The chair is beside the table.

examples.target: Tedd a széket az asztal mellé!
examples.en: Put the chair next to the table!

examples.target: A macska kijött az ágy alól.
examples.en: The cat came out from under the bed.

rules.title: Postpositions with personal endings
rules.body: Postpositions take the same personal endings as case suffixes on pronouns: mellettem (beside me), melletted, mellette, mellettünk, mellettetek, mellettük; előttem, utánam, mögöttünk, nélküled, miattam, helyettem, szerintem (in my opinion).

examples.en: In my opinion it is a good film.
I am not going without you.

rules.title: Time expressions with postpositions
rules.body: Several postpositions are mainly used with time: óta (since: hétfő óta), múlva (in, after a period from now: két óra múlva), alatt (during, within: egy hét alatt), előtt (before: ebéd előtt), után (after), közben (during, while: ebéd közben), körül (around: nyolc körül). 'Ago' is -val/-vel ezelőtt: két évvel ezelőtt.

examples.en: He has been ill since Monday.
I learnt it within a week.

exercises.explain: The v of -vel assimilates to the final r: Péterrel.
-val after busz gives busszal, with the sz doubled (ssz).
After a vowel -val attaches directly and the final a lengthens.

exercises.q: In -val/-vel the v assimilates to a preceding consonant: kés + -vel = késsel.
exercises.explain: The consonant is doubled in writing: késsel, kézzel, Péterrel.
-ért expresses purpose: elmegyek kenyérért.

exercises.q: Elmegyek ___. (I am going out for milk; tej)
exercises.explain: -ért has a single form: tejért.
-ig marks the end point in time.

exercises.q: Budapesttől ___ (from Budapest as far as Szeged)
exercises.explain: -ig = as far as; it never changes form.
-ig is one of the few suffixes with a single invariable form.
-ként means 'as, in the capacity of'.
Languages take -ul/-ül: magyarul, angolul, németül.
-kor gives the time at which something happens.

exercises.answer: A bolt a posta mellett van.
exercises.en: The shop is next to the post office.

exercises.explain: előtt = in front of; mögött = behind; alatt = under.

exercises.q: A macska az asztal ___ van. (The cat is under the table.)
exercises.explain: Static position under something is alatt.

exercises.q: Postpositions come after the noun and the noun takes no case ending: a ház mögött.
exercises.explain: The noun stays in its basic form before a postposition.

exercises.q: 'Put it next to the chair' needs which form?
exercises.explain: Movement towards a position takes the -é form: mellé.

exercises.q: A kutya kijött az asztal ___. (The dog came out from under the table.)
exercises.explain: Movement away from under something is alól.
-em is the first person ending: mögöttem.
után takes personal endings: utánam, utánad, utána.

exercises.en: After lunch we go for a walk.

exercises.explain: múlva means 'in (a period from now)'; 'ago' is két órával ezelőtt.
óta = since.

exercises.q: Nem tudok ___ élni. (I cannot live without you; nélkül + 'you')
exercises.explain: nélkül with the second person ending is nélküled.
miatt = because of; helyett = instead of; szerint = according to.

exercises.en: Péter is going to the cinema with Anna.

exercises.explain: miért is literally 'for what'.

sections.title: Adjectives, comparison and adverbs
sections.summary: Adjectives before a noun never change; after 'to be' they agree in number. Comparison uses -bb and leg-, and most adverbs are made with -an/-en.

rules.title: Adjectives before a noun do not change
rules.body: An attributive adjective stands before the noun and takes no ending at all, whatever the number or case of the noun: a nagy ház, a nagy házak, a nagy házban. Only when the adjective is the predicate (after 'to be') or stands alone does it take endings: A házak nagyok.

rules.title: Predicate adjectives agree in number
rules.body: After a plural subject a predicate adjective takes the plural -k with the usual linking vowels: nagyok, szépek, kicsik, drágák, olcsók, fáradtak, okosak. Adjectives ending in -ú/-ű and some in -i take -ak/-ek: hosszúak, könnyűek, régiek.

rules.title: The comparative -bb
rules.body: The comparative adds -bb: directly after a vowel (olcsó – olcsóbb, drága – drágább with lengthening), with a linking vowel after a consonant (nagy – nagyobb, magas – magasabb, okos – okosabb). Irregular: jó – jobb, sok – több, kicsi – kisebb, szép – szebb, hosszú – hosszabb, könnyű – könnyebb, bő – bővebb.

rules.title: 'Than': mint or -nál/-nél
rules.body: The second term of a comparison is introduced by mint (with a comma before it) or marked with -nál/-nél: Péter magasabb, mint Anna. Péter magasabb Annánál. 'Much' before a comparative is sokkal, 'a little' is egy kicsit or kicsit.

rules.title: The superlative leg-
rules.body: The superlative puts leg- in front of the comparative and normally takes the definite article: a legnagyobb, a legszebb, a legjobb, a legtöbb. 'The very best of all' can be intensified as a legeslegjobb.

rules.title: Adverbs: -an/-en and -ul/-ül
rules.body: Most adverbs of manner are formed with -an/-en after a consonant and -n after a vowel: gyors – gyorsan, szép – szépen, lassú – lassan (with shortening), olcsó – olcsón, drága – drágán. A few take -ul/-ül: rossz – rosszul. jó becomes jól and nagy becomes nagyon (very). -lag/-leg appears in some: valószínűleg (probably).

rules.title: Comparing adverbs
rules.body: Adverbs are compared by adding -an/-en to the comparative or superlative adjective: gyorsabban (faster), leggyorsabban (fastest), szebben, jobban (better), legjobban, többet (more, as in 'studies more'), kevesebbet (less).

examples.target: Anna jobban beszél magyarul, mint én.
examples.en: Anna speaks Hungarian better than I do.

rules.title: Equality and intensifiers
rules.body: 'As ... as' is olyan ... mint, or ugyanolyan ... mint for exact sameness. 'The more ..., the more' is minél ... annál. Useful intensifiers: nagyon (very), túl (too), elég (fairly, enough), egészen (quite), egyre + comparative (more and more).

examples.en: He is as tall as me.

examples.target: Minél többet tanulsz, annál többet tudsz.
examples.en: The more you study, the more you know.
It is getting better and better.

rules.title: Making adjectives: -s, -i, -talan/-telen
rules.body: -s (-os/-es/-ös/-as) means 'having, characterised by': sós (salty), cukros (sugary), esős (rainy), homokos (sandy). -i means 'relating to, from': budapesti, londoni, mai (today's), tegnapi (yesterday's), esti (evening). -talan/-telen (-tlan/-tlen) means 'without': boldogtalan (unhappy), ismeretlen (unknown), sótlan (unsalted). Asking about adjectives: Milyen? (what is it like?) and Melyik? (which one?).

examples.target: Milyen a ház? – Nagy és régi.
examples.en: What is the house like? – Big and old.

exercises.explain: An adjective before the noun takes no ending; 'a ház nagy' is a sentence, 'the house is big'.

exercises.q: An adjective standing before a plural noun takes no plural ending: nagy házak.
exercises.explain: Only predicate adjectives agree: A házak nagyok.

exercises.q: A házak ___. (The houses are big; nagy)
exercises.explain: After a plural subject the predicate adjective takes -k.
After a vowel -bb attaches directly.
After a consonant a linking vowel precedes -bb: nagyobb.
The comparative plus mint (or -nál/-nél on the second term).
The standard of comparison can take -nál/-nél instead of mint.
leg- is added to the irregular comparative szebb.
jó – jobb – a legjobb.

exercises.q: The superlative is formed with leg- plus the comparative form.
exercises.explain: nagy – nagyobb – legnagyobb.
gyors is a back word, so the adverb ending is -an.
Front words take -en: szépen.
jól (well) is irregular.
The adverb adds -an to the comparative: jobban.
jól – jobban – legjobban.
sokkal = much; 'a little bigger' is kicsit nagyobb.
Equality uses olyan ... mint.
sokkal, literally 'with much', intensifies a comparative.
The suffix -s means 'having, full of'.

exercises.q: Milyen a ház? – ___. (What is the house like? – Big.)
exercises.explain: Milyen? asks for a describing adjective.
Adjectives in -ú/-ű drop the long vowel: hosszabb, könnyebb.
The final ű is replaced by the linking vowel: könnyebb.
The long ú is dropped before -an: lassan.
leg- attaches to the comparative drágább, not to the base form.

exercises.answer: Minél többet tanulsz, annál többet tudsz.
exercises.en: The more you study, the more you know.

sections.title: Past tense and future
sections.summary: Hungarian has a single past tense built with -t/-tt, used for all English past forms, and expresses the future with the present tense, with fog + infinitive, or with majd and lesz.

rules.title: The past marker -t / -ott / -ett / -ött
rules.body: The past is marked by -t, sometimes with a linking vowel, before the personal endings. Group 1 takes plain -t in all persons: stems ending in a vowel plus j, l, ly, n, ny or r (vár – várt, tanul – tanult, kér – kért). Group 2 takes -ott/-ett/-ött only in the third person singular and plain -t elsewhere: most other stems (olvastam but olvasott, mondtam but mondott, néztem but nézett). Group 3 takes -ott/-ett/-ött in every person: stems in -ít, in two consonants plus t, and most stems in a short vowel plus t (tanítottam, értettem, szerettem, futottam). lát is an exception: láttam, látott.

rules.title: Past indefinite endings
rules.body: After the past marker, the indefinite endings are -am/-em (I), -ál/-él (you), nothing (he/she), -unk/-ünk (we), -atok/-etek (you plural), -ak/-ek (they). The third person singular is just the past stem.

examples.target: vártam, vártál, várt, vártunk, vártatok, vártak
examples.en: I waited, you waited, he waited, we waited, you waited, they waited

examples.target: kértem, kértél, kért, kértünk, kértetek, kértek
examples.en: I asked for, you asked for, ...

rules.title: Past definite endings
rules.body: With a definite object the endings are -am/-em (I), -ad/-ed (you), -a/-e (he/she), -uk/-ük (we), -átok/-étek (you plural), -ák/-ék (they). The first person singular is identical in both conjugations. The 'I ... you' ending is -alak/-elek: vártalak, szerettelek.

examples.target: vártam, vártad, várta, vártuk, vártátok, várták
examples.en: I waited for it, you waited for it, ...

rules.title: Irregular pasts
rules.body: The common irregular verbs have special past stems: van – volt (voltam, voltál, volt, voltunk, voltatok, voltak), megy – ment (mentem), jön – jött (jöttem), eszik – evett (ettem, ettél, evett, ettünk), iszik – ivott (ittam, ittál, ivott), tesz – tett, vesz – vett, visz – vitt, hisz – hitt, alszik – aludt (aludtam), fekszik – feküdt, lesz – lett (became).

examples.en: Yesterday we went to the cinema.

rules.title: One past tense for everything
rules.body: The single past covers English 'I worked', 'I was working', 'I have worked' and 'I had worked'. Completion is signalled instead by a verbal prefix: írtam a levelet (I was writing the letter) versus megírtam a levelet (I wrote the letter and finished it). Typical past time words: tegnap (yesterday), tavaly (last year), múlt héten (last week), régen (long ago), már (already), még nem (not yet).

examples.en: I have not seen it yet.

rules.title: The future with fog + infinitive
rules.body: A definite future uses the auxiliary fog with the infinitive. fog is conjugated like a normal verb in both the indefinite (fogok, fogsz, fog, fogunk, fogtok, fognak) and the definite set (fogom, fogod, fogja, fogjuk, fogjátok, fogják), chosen by the object of the infinitive. In a neutral sentence the infinitive, or the verbal prefix, stands before fog: Dolgozni fogok. Meg fogom nézni.

rules.title: Future with the present tense and majd
rules.body: Very often the plain present tense with a time word expresses the future: Holnap megyek. The adverb majd (later, then, at some point) also points to the future and is typical of promises and vague plans: Majd meglátjuk. Majd hívlak.

rules.title: lesz: the future of van
rules.body: The future of 'to be' is lesz (leszek, leszel, lesz, leszünk, lesztek, lesznek), which also means 'become'. It replaces van in 'to have' sentences about the future, and volt replaces it in the past: Lesz időm. Volt egy kutyám. Nem volt pénzem.

rules.title: 'Ago', 'in', 'for'
rules.body: 'Two years ago' is két évvel ezelőtt or simply két éve; 'in two hours' is két óra múlva; 'for two years' (and still) is két éve with the present tense: Két éve tanulok magyarul. Clock times take -kor in every tense: ötkor jöttem.

examples.en: I came to Hungary two years ago.
I have been learning Hungarian for three years.

exercises.explain: Past marker -t plus the first person ending -am.
kér is a group 1 verb: kért + -em.
Stems in l take plain -t; tanulta would be the definite form.

exercises.q: The third person singular of the past indefinite has no personal ending: várt.
exercises.explain: The bare past stem is the he/she form.
Group 2 verbs take -ott/-ett/-ött in the third person singular only.
olvas takes plain -t outside the third person singular: olvastam.
-ít verbs take the linking vowel in every person: tanítottam.
A stem in a short vowel plus t takes -ett in all persons: szeret + ett + em.
The past stem of van is volt; lettem means 'I became'.
volt + -ál: voltál.
megy has the irregular past stem ment.
jön has the past stem jött: jöttem, jöttél, jött.

exercises.q: Hungarian has only one past tense, covering 'I worked', 'I was working' and 'I have worked'.
exercises.explain: Aspect is shown by verbal prefixes and context, not by tense.
The first person singular is the same in both conjugations; 'a könyvet' makes the sentence match.

exercises.q: ___ a filmet? (Did you (singular) see the film? lát)
exercises.explain: Definite object, second person: lát + t + ad.
The definite 'we' ending in the past is -uk/-ük: írtuk.
-elek after the past marker is the 'I ... you' ending.
fog is conjugated and the verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.q: Holnap esni ___. (It will rain tomorrow; fog, third person)
exercises.explain: The third person singular of fog has no ending.
fog takes the definite ending because 'a filmet' is definite: fogjuk.

exercises.q: Holnap hideg ___. (It will be cold tomorrow; future of van)
exercises.explain: lesz is the future of 'to be'.

exercises.q: 'Holnap megyek' uses the present tense to talk about the future.
exercises.explain: With a time word the present is the normal way to express the future.
-val/-vel ezelőtt = ago; múlva = in (from now).

exercises.q: Nem ___ időm. (I had no time; past of van)
exercises.explain: The past of nincs is nem volt.
Stems in a short vowel plus t take -ott: futott.

exercises.q: 'Megírtam a levelet' implies the letter was finished, while 'Írtam a levelet' does not.
exercises.explain: The prefix meg- marks completion.

sections.title: Questions, negation, word order and focus
sections.summary: Word order in Hungarian is governed by focus: the emphasised element stands right before the verb and pushes the verbal prefix behind it. This chapter also covers negation, the -e particle, numbers and telling the time.

rules.title: Yes/no questions and the -e particle
rules.body: A yes/no question keeps the word order of the statement and is marked only by intonation, which rises on the second-to-last syllable and falls on the last: Jössz? The particle -e is attached to the verb in indirect questions and in formal or written direct questions: Nem tudom, hogy jön-e. The tag ugye? asks for agreement. Short answers repeat the verb: Jössz? – Jövök. / Nem.

examples.en: I don't know whether he is at home.

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: ki? (who), mi? (what), hol? (where), hová? (where to), honnan? (where from), mikor? (when), miért? (why), hogy? or hogyan? (how), mennyi? (how much), hány? (how many), milyen? (what kind), melyik? (which). Question words take case endings like nouns: kit?, kinek?, kivel?, mit?, miről?. The question word stands immediately before the verb.

rules.title: Negation with nem, nincs and sem
rules.body: nem stands directly before the verb, or before the word it negates: Nem tudom. Nem én voltam. nincs/nincsenek negate van/vannak. sem means 'not ... either, neither' and follows the word it belongs to: Én sem. Hungarian uses multiple negation: the negative pronouns senki (nobody), semmi (nothing), soha (never), sehol (nowhere) are combined with nem or sem.

rules.title: Neutral word order
rules.body: A neutral sentence runs topic, verb, then the rest: Péter megírta a levelet. The subject need not come first, and a known element (the topic) can be moved to the front. A verbal prefix such as meg-, el-, fel-, ki-, be- is written together with the verb in a neutral sentence: elmegy, megnézi, felkel.

examples.en: The children went off to school.
I get up at seven in the morning.

rules.title: Focus: the slot before the verb
rules.body: The element you want to stress, the new or contrasted information, stands immediately before the verb, in the focus position. When something is in focus, a verbal prefix detaches and moves after the verb: Péter a levelet írta meg (it was the letter that Péter wrote). Péter írta meg a levelet (it was Péter who wrote it). Question words and negated elements are always in focus.

examples.en: It was the letter that Péter wrote.
It was Péter who wrote the letter.
It is tomorrow that I am leaving.

rules.title: nem, question words and prefixes
rules.body: Because nem and question words occupy the focus slot, they also split the prefix from the verb: Nem írta meg. Mikor ment el? The same happens with csak (only) and with the fog future: Meg fogom nézni. Only in neutral sentences does the prefix stay attached.

rules.title: is and sem
rules.body: is (also, too) is a separate word placed right after the word it refers to: Én is megyek (I'm going too). Péter is jön. Its negative partner is sem: Én sem megyek. Péter sem jön. Both can attach to any element in the sentence, which changes the meaning: Péter is kávét iszik (Péter too) versus Péter kávét is iszik (coffee as well).

rules.title: Numbers
rules.body: 1-10: egy, kettő (két before a noun), három, négy, öt, hat, hét, nyolc, kilenc, tíz. 11-19: tizenegy, tizenkettő ... tizenkilenc. 20 húsz, 21 huszonegy; 30 harminc, 40 negyven, 50 ötven, 60 hatvan, 70 hetven, 80 nyolcvan, 90 kilencven, 100 száz, 1000 ezer. Numbers above 2000 are hyphenated after ezer: kétezer-huszonhat. Ordinals: első, második, then -dik: harmadik, negyedik, ötödik, hatodik, hetedik, nyolcadik, kilencedik, tizedik. The noun after a number is singular.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Hány óra (van)? or Mennyi az idő? asks the time. Öt óra van (it's five o'clock). The half and quarter hours count towards the coming hour: fél hat is 5:30 (half of the sixth hour), negyed hat is 5:15, háromnegyed hat is 5:45. Minutes: öt perccel múlt hat (five past six), tíz perc múlva hét (ten to seven). 'At' a time takes -kor: ötkor, fél hatkor, háromnegyed hatkor.

examples.en: What time is it? – Half past five.
I get up at a quarter past seven.
It starts at a quarter to nine.

rules.title: Days, parts of the day and polite requests
rules.body: 'On' a day uses -n: hétfőn, kedden, szerdán, csütörtökön, pénteken, szombaton, but vasárnap (on Sunday) takes no ending. Months take -ban/-ben: májusban. Parts of the day: reggel (in the morning), délelőtt, délben (at noon), délután, este, éjjel. Polite requests use Kérek + accusative (I'd like), Szeretnék + infinitive (I would like to), Legyen szíves (please, formal) and Tessék (here you are / go ahead).

examples.en: On Monday I work, on Sunday I rest.

exercises.q: The usual spoken way to ask 'Are you coming?':
exercises.explain: A yes/no question keeps the statement form and uses intonation.

exercises.q: Yes/no questions keep the word order of the statement and are marked by intonation.
exercises.explain: Jössz? (Are you coming?) has the same words as Jössz. (You are coming.)

exercises.q: Nem tudom, hogy ___. (I don't know whether he is coming; jön + particle)
exercises.explain: Indirect yes/no questions attach -e to the verb.
hol = where (static); hová = where to; honnan = where from.
nem stands directly before the verb.
nem negates the verb vagyok; nincs is only for van/vannak.
Negative pronouns are combined with nem (or sem): Senki nem jött.

exercises.q: Hungarian uses double negation: 'Soha nem eszem húst.'
exercises.explain: soha (never) still requires nem before the verb.

exercises.q: Én ___. (Me neither; the negative counterpart of 'is')
exercises.explain: sem = not ... either; Én sem.

exercises.q: The neutral sentence 'Péter wrote the letter' (no special emphasis):
exercises.explain: In a neutral sentence the prefix stays attached; the other two put the letter or Péter in focus.

exercises.q: In 'Péter a levelet írta meg', what is emphasised?
options: the letter (it was the letter that he wrote)
exercises.explain: The element right before the verb is in focus, and the prefix meg has moved after it.

exercises.q: When something is in focus, the verbal prefix moves after the verb: 'Nem írta meg.'
exercises.explain: nem occupies the focus slot and detaches the prefix.

exercises.q: Mikor ___ el? (When did he leave? elmegy, past)
exercises.explain: The question word is in focus, so el follows the verb: Mikor ment el?
öt = 5, hat = 6, hét = 7.
Teens are tizen- plus the unit: tizenegy.
két is used before a noun, and the noun stays singular.
Ordinals from three onwards end in -dik with a linking vowel.
fél hat is half of the sixth hour, i.e. half past five.

exercises.q: negyed ___ (5:15, a quarter of the sixth hour)
exercises.explain: Quarter hours count towards the coming hour: negyed hat = 5:15.
Three quarters of the sixth hour have passed.
Days take -n: hétfőn, kedden, szombaton.
vasárnap is the one day that takes no ending for 'on'.
-kor marks the time at which something happens.

exercises.q: ___ egy kávét. (I'd like a coffee; the polite 'I ask for')
exercises.explain: Kérek + accusative is the standard polite way to order.
